title: The Philidor defence
summary: Draw rook against rook and pawn by holding the third rank and, once the pawn advances, checking from behind.
step.take: First you have to get there. Your king is already on the queening square, but the rook is on the first rank. Bring it to the third and, as long as Black does not advance the pawn, keep strolling along it.
step.take.hint: 1.Rb3. Then a waiting move on the same rank: 2.Ra3.
step.take.done: The rank is yours. Notice that you do not need to do anything: it is Black who has to act.
step.behind.hint: 1.Ra8. After 1...Kf3, 2.Rf8+; and after each king move, check on the file where it stands.
step.endgame.done: With the king on e1, in front of the pawn, the black king cannot drive it out: if the pawn advances with check, you step back in front of it and it is stalemate. Retreating sideways, to d1 or f1, would lose.
step.t_classic: This is the Philidor position, and you defend with White. Before I explain: what stops the black king from advancing, and what can Black still try?
step.t_classic.hint1: Look at the rank your rook is on. Which squares does it deny the black king?
step.t_bishop: Now a bishop's pawn, with the pieces scattered. Black threatens to bring the king in. Which move sets up the defence?
step.t_bishop.hint1: The recipe does not depend on the pawn: find the rank the black king cannot cross.
ex.e15: The black king is ready to step onto your third rank, and your rook attacks the pawn. What is the move? Find the draw.
ex.e15.hint: The pawn is protected. What stops the black king from advancing in the Philidor position? Your rook is one move away from it.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Rg3: the rook takes the third rank and it is the Philidor position. Going to the far end of the file (1.Rg5, 1.Rg6, 1.Rg7, 1.Rg8) also holds, but the third rank is the simple way. King moves lose: the black king walks into d3. 1.Rxe4+?? gives the rook away, because the black king protects the pawn. In the rook endgame practice, chapter "Avoiding the Philidor", this position appears with the other side to move: the attacker moves first and wins.
ex.e12: The Philidor defence against a d-pawn, and the black rook checks along the first rank. Where does the king go? Find the draw.
ex.e12.hint: Before you pick the square, see which one lets the pawn advance with check.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Kd2 (or 1.Kc2). 1.Ke2? loses: 1...d3+! The pawn advances with check, gains the tempo it needed, and the black king walks onto the third rank. On d2 the king stays in front of the pawn, goes back to d1 at the next check, and the rook keeps the third rank. A training position by Audax6.
ex.e11: A position Philidor analysed in 1777, with the colours reversed. Your rook is not on the third rank yet, and the black king wants to step into e3. How do you get there in time? Find the draw.
ex.e11.hint: The f-file is a trap: on f3 the pawn captures the rook, and at the far end of the file the rook stops nothing. Look for another road to the third rank.
ex.e11.solution: 1.Rb5! (1.Rg5 and 1.Rh5 work too): the rook runs along the fifth rank and drops down next move. If 1...Ke3, 2.Rb3+, and the black king has to go back behind the line: it is the Philidor position (2.Kf1 also held). 1.Rf8? loses to 1...Ke3, the hasty mistake from the lesson, and 2.Rf3?? drops the rook: 2...exf3. The king moves 1.Kd1 and 1.Kf1 also hold, but they do not build the defence.
ex.e16: A bishop pawn, your king next to the queening square and your rook still on the first rank. The black king threatens to step onto your third rank. Find the draw.
ex.e16.hint: King first, in front of the pawn. If the black king steps onto the third rank anyway, look for a check that sends it back and leaves the rook where it needs to be.
ex.e16.solution: 1.Kc1!, the only move: the king goes to the queening square. If 1...Kc3, 2.Re3+!, again the only move: the black king has to go back behind the third rank, and the rook is already on it. It is the Philidor position. On the first move, 1.Re3?? drops the rook to the black king, and the other moves lose because the black king gets in first. Our own position.
ex.e14: A bishop pawn, your king still far from the queening square and the black rook already on your third rank. Reach the Philidor defence. Find the draw.
ex.e14.hint: The king goes in front of the pawn first. But the shortest road puts king and rook on the same rank, and the black rook likes that.
ex.e14.solution: 1.Kd2! The direct 1.Kd1? loses to 1...Rb1+: the check hits the king and, behind it, the rook on e1. After 1...Rb2+, 2.Kc1! (2.Kd1? Rb1+ again). With the king on c1, the queening square, the rook takes the third rank: 3.Re3, and it is the Philidor position (3.Re5, 3.Re6, 3.Re7 and 3.Re8 also hold). King first, then the rook, and no skewer. Our own position.
history: This is the most important defence in rook endings: with rook against rook and pawn, it is the simplest way to draw. {{François-André Philidor|francois-andre-philidor}}, a composer and the best chess player of his time, published it in 1777 and believed it was the only way to save the game. For more than a century books repeated his analysis, mistake included: Philidor called some positions lost that were still drawn, as the German Max Karstedt showed in 1897. Even so, the third-rank defence is still the first one every player should know by heart, because it saves half a point in a great many games.
practice: Now the practical challenge: you have only the rook, your opponent has the rook and the pawn. Take the third rank, wait for the pawn to advance and check from behind. The goal is to draw.
part.third.title: The Philidor position
part.third.summary: King on the queening square, rook on the third rank, and you wait. It is Black who has to take a risk.
part.side.title: Side checks
part.side.summary: Against checks from the side, the king stays in front of the pawn and away from the square where the pawn advances with check.
part.behind.title: Checks from behind
part.behind.summary: On the very move the pawn steps onto the third rank, the rook goes to the far end and keeps checking.
part.reach.title: Third rank in time
part.reach.summary: Get the rook to the third rank before the black king arrives. With the pawn still on the fourth, checking is too early.
part.kingFirst.title: King first
part.kingFirst.summary: With the king far from the queening square, it goes first, without giving the black rook a check that hits king and rook.
part.expel.title: Driving the king off
part.expel.summary: If the black king has already stepped onto the third rank, a check along it sends the king back and leaves the rook in place.
part.trade.title: The rook trade
part.trade.summary: If Black blocks the check with the rook, trade rooks, and in the pawn ending retreat the king straight back.
part.beyond.title: Other pawns
part.beyond.summary: The same defence against a bishop's pawn and the three rules to take into your games.
step.t_classic.hint2: Now imagine Black only shuffles the rook back and forth. Do you need to do anything?
step.intro: {{François-André Philidor|francois-andre-philidor}}, the strongest player of the 18th century, analysed this position in 1777, and it has three pieces in place. Your king on e1, the pawn's queening square. Your rook on the third rank, from end to end. And the black king behind that line: as long as the rook is there, it cannot step onto e3, f3 or g3, and without the king in front the pawn does not get through.
step.d_wait: Watch how this position is defended: by waiting. Black moves first.
step.d_wait.m1: 1...Rb2. The black rook changes square looking for a way in, but it threatens nothing: the black king still cannot use the third rank.
step.d_wait.m2: 2.Rc3. Your rook moves too, without leaving the third rank: any square the black pieces cannot capture it on will do, because from there it keeps barring e3, f3 and g3.
step.d_wait.m3: 2...Ra2. Another move with no progress. Black cannot drive your rook off the rank or get the king past it.
step.d_wait.m4: 3.Rb3, and you answer the same way. You need no plan: it is Black who has to come up with something, and all that is left is to advance the pawn.
step.t_side: The black rook has given check along the first rank. Your rook is on the third, where it belongs. Where does the king go, and what does it need to keep doing?
step.t_side.hint1: The king does not need to run far away: its job is to stay in front of the pawn.
step.side: Against checks along the first rank, the king steps up one square and stays in front of the pawn: e2, and back to e1 at the next check. The rook does not leave the third rank, because it is what holds the black king back. With the pawn on e4, even d2 or f2 would do. But there is one square that never works: the one where the pawn advances with check.
step.d_sideTrap: With a bishop's pawn the trap appears. The white king was on c1, got checked and went to d2, which looks natural: it stays close to the pawn.
step.d_sideTrap.m1: 1...c3+! The pawn advances with check. The move you would spend getting out of check is the tempo the black king needed to walk onto the third rank, and the defence is over.
step.sideHold: The same position, with the king on c1 and the check given. Pick the square where the pawn cannot advance with check and, at the next check, go back in front of it.
step.sideHold.hint: 1.Kc2: there the pawn cannot advance with check. After 1...Rh2+, 2.Kc1.
step.sideHold.done: The king goes back and forth between c1 and c2, and the rook never leaves the third rank. Before answering a check, ask: on this square, does the pawn advance with check?
step.t_pawn: Back to the Philidor position, a few moves later: Black got tired of waiting and pushed the pawn to e3. Your rook is still on the third rank. What has changed, and where does it go now?
step.t_pawn.hint1: Can your rook still see f3? What is in the way?
step.t_pawn.hint2: Against checks from behind, where would the black king hide? Who occupies that square now?
step.pawn: The pawn on e3 closes the third rank: your rook no longer reaches f3, and the black king threatens to walk in there and mate along the first rank. But the advance has a price. The e3 square, which would shelter the black king from checks from behind, now belongs to its own pawn. So the rook leaves the rank and goes to the far end of the board.
step.d_behind: Watch the checks from behind, move by move.
step.d_behind.m1: 1.Rb8! The rook goes to the far end, as far from the black king as possible, so the king cannot come close to it and escape the checks.
step.d_behind.m2: 1...Kf3. The black king walks in, and the threat is 2...Ra1+: blocking with 3.Rb1 does not help, 3...Rxb1 is mate.
step.d_behind.m3: 2.Rf8+. The check comes from behind, along the king's file. That is why the rook had to be far away.
step.d_behind.m4: 2...Ke4. The black king wanted to hide in front of the pawn, on e3, but that square is taken. It has to step back.
step.d_behind.m5: 3.Re8+. Another check, now along the pawn's file: if the black king walks away from it, the rook is already aiming at the pawn on e3.
step.d_behind.m6: 3...Kf4. It stays next to the pawn to protect it, and that is why it cannot escape the checks.
step.d_behind.m8: 4...Ke5. Going up does not help: the king has left the pawn and is still far from your rook.
step.d_behind.m9: 5.Re8+. The black king has no square that does not lead to another check or leave the pawn undefended. A draw.
step.d_passive: Now the opposite mistake: staying. The pawn advanced and, instead of going to the far end, the rook stayed on the third rank, on c3.
step.d_passive.m1: 1...Kf3, and the black king is in. The threat is 2...Ra1+, and blocking with 3.Rc1 does not help: 3...Rxc1 is mate. One move late, and the defence is gone.
step.behind: Now you, in a similar position, with the black rook on h2. The pawn has just stepped onto the third rank. Rook to the far end and, when the black king walks in, checks along its file.
step.behind.done: The black king has no shelter. If it walks away from the pawn, the rook attacks the pawn; if it comes back, more checks. Third rank until the pawn advances, then checks from behind.
step.t_reach: This position comes from a rook endgame training collection that NoseKnowsAll put together on Lichess; here the colours are reversed. The black king wants to step into e3, and your rook is still far away, on the seventh rank. How do you reach the Philidor defence in time?
step.t_reach.hint1: Which square does the black king want, and which rank takes it away?
step.t_reach.hint2: A check is tempting. But think about what the black king does after it, with the pawn still on the fourth rank.
step.d_early: First, the mistake. White checked right away: 1.Rd7+.
step.d_early.m1: 1...Ke3! The black king steps in next to the pawn, on the square the pawn has not taken yet. Now the pawn on e4 shields it from checks from above: 2.Rd3+ just gives the rook away. And the threat is 2...Rh1, mate.
step.reachWhy: The rule is this: the rook reaches the third rank before the black king does and leaves it only after the pawn steps onto it. With the pawn still on the fourth, a check from behind is too early, because the black king has a square next to the pawn to hide on.
step.reach: Now the right way, in the same position. Bring the rook to the third rank and, when the pawn advances, do what you have already seen.
step.reach.hint: 1.Ra3. After 1...e3, the rook goes to the far end: 2.Ra8.
step.reach.done: Rook on the third before the black king, and to the far end when the pawn stepped onto it. That is the whole defence, arriving in time.
step.t_king: Now your king is far from the queening square, on g2, and the black rook already sits on your third rank. Where do you start?
step.t_king.hint1: Which white piece is out of place for the Philidor defence?
step.t_king.hint2: Careful with the first rank: king and rook side by side on it are a target for the black rook.
step.d_skewer: First, the mistake. 1.Kf1 looks like the shortest road to e1.
step.d_skewer.m1: 1...Rd1+! King and rook on the same rank. If the king steps away, the rook on g1 falls. If it goes to g2 to protect it, Black trades rooks, and the pawn ending is lost because your king is far from the pawn. That is the skewer.
step.kingWhy: When the king is far away, it goes first: it is the king that has to stand in front of the pawn. The rook waits on the first rank, which nothing threatens yet. And the king's road must not leave it on the same rank as the rook while the black rook can check along that rank.
step.kingFirst: The same position. King first, by the safe road; when it reaches the queening square, the rook takes the third rank.
step.kingFirst.hint: 1.Kf2. After the check, 2.Ke1. Then the rook climbs the g-file to the third rank.
step.kingFirst.done: King on e1, rook on g3: it is the Philidor position. The order made the difference: king first, then the rook.
step.t_expel: The black king has already stepped onto your third rank, on e3, and your rook is still on h1. It looks too late. Is there a move that holds?
step.t_expel.hint1: Look for a check that does not take the rook off the rank where it needs to be.
step.d_expel.m1: 1.Rh3+! The check comes along the third rank: the black king has to leave it, and the rook already stands where it needs to be.
step.d_expel.m2: 1...Kd4. The king goes back behind the line. The squares d2 and f2 belong to your king, and the third rank belongs to your rook.
step.d_expel.m3: 2.Rb3. The rook moves away from the black king without leaving the rank, and it is the Philidor position: king on the queening square, rook on the third, black king behind it.
step.expelWhy: Why does the check have to come along the third rank? Any other move leaves the black king on e3, and from there it never leaves. 1.Rh3+ does two things at once: it drives the black king off the rank and puts the rook on it.
step.expel: Now the black king came in through f3, and your rook is at the far end, on h8. Drive the king out and set up the defence.
step.expel.hint: 1.Rh3+, and then the rook stays on the third rank, away from the black king.
step.expel.done: The black king went back behind the line and the rook stayed on it. Getting to the third rank late is not always the end: a check along it can still put everything right.
step.t_trade: Black has put the rook on the fifth rank, on a5, ready to block your checks. What does Black want, and should you be afraid of it?
step.t_trade.hint1: If the black rook blocks the check, the rooks come off. The king and pawn ending that remains is good for whom?
step.trade: Black wants to block the checks with the rook and force the exchange. Do not be afraid. The king and pawn ending that remains is a draw, on one condition: your king retreats straight back, in front of the pawn.
step.d_trade.m1: 1.Rd8+. The usual check, along the king's file.
step.d_trade.m2: 1...Rd5. Black blocks with the rook, and your rook is attacked.
step.d_trade.m3: 2.Rxd5+. Trade without fear: this is the pawn ending you want.
step.d_trade.m4: 2...Kxd5. King and pawn against king is left. The pawn is on your third rank and your king is next to the queening square: all that is left is to put the king on the right road.
step.endgame: Now you. Your king is on d1, next to the queening square. Hold the pawn ending.
step.endgame.hint: 1.Ke2, in front of the pawn. When the black king comes close, retreat straight back: 2.Ke1.
step.t_bishop.hint2: Black wants to step onto c3 or d3. Which rank takes those squares away?
step.bishop: The defence works against any pawn. This is a training position by Yuri61, with colours reversed: a bishop's pawn and the pieces scattered, but the recipe is the same. The rook takes the third rank. Here only two moves hold: that one, or the king straight to c1, the queening square, because Black threatens to walk in with the king.
step.bishopMove: Set up the defence with the rook.
step.bishopMove.hint: 1.Rg3: the rook on the third rank bars c3 and d3.
step.bishopMove.done: The same defence, another pawn. The king is next to the queening square and the rook closes the rank: Black is back to depending on the pawn advance.
step.recap: Three rules. One: king on the queening square and rook on the third rank, waiting; if the king is far away, it gets there first. Two: when the pawn steps onto the third rank, the rook goes to the far end and checks from behind; not before, not after. Three: if the rooks come off, the king retreats straight back, in front of the pawn. And when the third rank no longer works, there is another defence: it is the short-side lesson.
step.finish: Now the practical challenge, from the start. You know the order: first the rank, then patience, and the checks only at the right moment.
key.classic: Philidor's position, from 1777: the white king on the square where the pawn wants to promote and the rook on the third rank, barring the black king. A draw, whoever moves.
key.reach: The white rook is not on the third rank yet. The first step is to get it there before the black king arrives.
key.bishop: Against a bishop pawn the defence is the same: the rook goes to the third rank and waits.
key.advanced: Here the rook can no longer reach the third rank in time. It goes to the far end of the board and, once the pawn advances, starts checking from behind.
